description: I'm Minh Hoang Tran, a second-year AI student in the UTS–Bach Khoa TNE program. I'm forming a team to investigate water and climate trends using NASA data and assess water-related risks for AI infrastructure. I'm seeking teammates interested in Python, data analysis, geospatial visualization, web development, or UX/UI design. Together, we'll build a practical, evidence-based prototype through open collaboration.

details:
The Rovers We Left Behind is an eight-page illustrated English story designed for readers aged 9-13. It introduces two examples of NASA hardware left on other worlds: the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle on the Moon and Opportunity on Mars.

Readers follow clearly labelled fictional rover voices alongside separate NASA fact passages. The Apollo chapter explains how a vehicle helped astronauts explore and carry equipment and lunar samples. The Opportunity chapter explains robotic exploration, evidence of ancient water, solar power, and the end of communications. The story distinguishes evidence of past water from proof of life.

Credited NASA photographs, photo mosaics, and a labelled NASA scientific dust simulation connect the narrative to real missions. A short quiz, answer key, and museum-label writing activity help readers compare the hardware and practise separating observation, interpretation, and fiction. References support further reading.

ChatGPT/Codex supplied the working concept and assisted with research, factual checking, narration, activity design, layout, submission text, and authoring code. Python and python-docx produced the editable story. The demo used @oai/artifact-tool. Microsoft Word and PowerPoint exported the final PDFs. No AI-generated image, audio, or video assets are included.

The completed deliverables are the story PDF, editable Word source, seven-slide demo PDF, editable PowerPoint, and source and image credits. This is a reading resource, not an application. Its intended benefit is to help young readers connect space equipment with the science it enabled. No classroom testing or measured learning improvement is claimed.
